. On 9 and 10 September, a swarm of approximately 24 Russian drones launched from four different Russian sites and entered Polish airspace. The drones were made of plywood and Styrofoam and are estimated to have cost €10,000 (approximately US$11,800) each. Several drones were shot down, some crashed, while a number travelled hundreds of kilometres deep into Poland. At least five of
the drones’ flight paths indicated they were headed towards Rzeszów-Jasionka Airport, a key NATO logistics hub – an act of deliberate intimidation
. The incursion occurred amid a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine.

Donald Tusk, Poland’s prime minister, described the incursion as a ‘large-scale provocation’ and Polish military command called it an ‘unprecedented violation’. NATO raised air policing and surveillance levels. Poland swiftly activated its air defences, with Polish F-16s and Dutch F-35s, supported by German Patriot systems and an Italian Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) surveillance aircraft. The Alliance has reinforced its posture under Eastern Sentry following the incident.
incursion was followed three days later by a Russian-made Geran drone violating Romanian airspace.

On 19 September, Estonia reported that three Russian MiG-31s entered its airspace over the Gulf of Finland for around 12 minutes. Moscow denied any violation, stating that the jets were transiting to Kaliningrad over international waters. Earlier this week drones closed Oslo and Copenhagen airports for several hours. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was the ‘most serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure to date’ and suggested the Danish authorities were keeping an open mind as to who was behind the incident.

The Kremlin’s playbook includes targeting critical national infrastructure both physically and through cyber attacks, recruiting proxies to limit its exposure and employing influence operations to undermine European security and manipulate public opinion. One aim of
Russia’s unconventional war on Europe is to normalise such incidents with the long-term objective of destabilising European societies.
Beyond drones, routine provocations include GPS jamming across the Baltic region, disruptions to air traffic and maritime operations.

The recent incursions into NATO’s airspace suggest a calculated escalation. Firstly, to identify potential vulnerabilities in NATO’s air defences, assess response times and gauge the Alliance’s resolve. Secondly, to spread insecurity, sow disunity among allies and erode public confidence in NATO’s ability to protect its citizens. Thirdly, the drone incursions forced NATO to expend expensive missiles against low-cost drones that, if repeated at scale, would strain Alliance inventories and budgets.

It is likely that the Kremlin was emboldened by perceptions of waning American interest in Europe, leading to more assertive foreign-policy actions, but the shift in rhetoric from United States’ President Donald Trump will force the Kremlin to recalibrate its approach. Trump’s suggestion that NATO states should shoot down any Russian aircraft that violate their airspace is in stark contrast to his earlier comments following the Russian drone incursion into Polish airspace that questioned the intent, stating it ‘could have been a mistake’ and remarking that he wasn’t ‘gonna defend anybody’. The Kremlin is likely to probe whether European air forces will act on new guidance without an explicit US backstop.

Following the drone incursion, Poland formally invoked Article 4 of the Washington Treaty, initiating urgent consultations among allies. NATO member states held formal consultations following Estonia’s request for the same – the second time in two weeks (and only the ninth time since NATO was formed in 1949).

NATO’s challenge is now to develop a sustainable response. Using fighters, AWACS and tanker aircraft as well as air-to-air missiles (Polish investigators are looking at whether a F-16 fired an AIM-120 at a drone, went off course and caused damage to a Polish domestic residence) to counter cheap €10,000 drones highlights a critical vulnerability. At scale, launching hundreds of inexpensive drones can quickly exhaust the Alliance’s finite and costly supply of interceptors, potentially leaving some sectors exposed while reloading. NATO officials have requested a 400% increase in air and missile-defence capabilities. One European NATO member state is reported to have acquired Apollo, a high-energy laser weapon built by Electro Optic Systems. Meanwhile, BAE has mooted the idea of adding the air-to-air optimised variant of the laser-guided Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System rocket to the Eurofighter Typhoon.
Beyond the military challenge, the recent slew of incidents has changed the political picture.
Six European countries have stated they will defend their airspace with force

. Lithuania, for example, has authorised its forces to shoot down unlawful drones in peacetime. Trump’s intervention will be welcomed by NATO allies, even if it came with the caveat that US support would depend on the circumstance. To that end, Russia will continue to actively seek to exploit divisions as such opportunities arrive.

Following numerous incursions, NATO member states have replaced ambiguity with clarity. Following Trump’s intervention, that clarity now has political top-cover even if it doesn’t come with an explicit US backstop. As NATO and European capitals stand up military forces, a cautionary precedent exists.
